caption:
Why does my skin get dry and irritated when the seasons change?
Korean has a word for that stretch of weeks: 환절기 (hwan-jeol-gi), the season-changing time.

It is used the way English uses "flu season" - a period when everyone expects the body to be a little off. For skin, it comes with habits that start before the weather turns, not after.

The moisturiser gets heavier first, before anything feels tight. A damp towel or a rack of laundry goes up indoors once the heating comes on - the old humidifier. Lip balm and hand cream appear on desks, because lips and hands usually crack first. And nothing new and strong gets started, because the skin is already adjusting.

There is a reason behind the timing. Measured across a year in 72 women in China, cheek skin held the least water and lost the most through its surface in winter.

What this is not: a treatment, or proof that any one habit works. It is how people here talk about, and prepare for, a change they know is coming. Skin that stings, flakes or flares for weeks is not "just the season".

No seasons where you live? Your 환절기 is the long flight, or the office air-conditioning.

Yang J et al. Skin Res Technol 2020. doi:10.1111/srt.12857

General education only.
